name: Dockmaster Vane
bio: Runs Keel Town's civic moorings — the resident sky-rafts, the market floats, the hang-tenant registry and its famous Window Three — from a ledgered office four hundred metres above the floor of everything. Devanna Shore runs the Guild's commercial masts and winch yards; Vane runs the town that clings to them, and the two maintain a professional rivalry conducted entirely through countersignature. Has not touched the ground in twenty-six years and plans to keep it that way; the ground, he maintains, is where paperwork goes to get sand in it.
appearance: Tall, thin man in his late fifties in a pale ochre harbour-master's coat with teal altitude piping, ink-stained cuffs, a brass barometer on a chain he consults like a wristwatch, boots with absurdly soft soles, leaning perpetually against a railing with one hand on the moorage line and the other on his stamp pad, the mesa's violet drop behind him.
voice: Airy, clipped, faintly winded even sitting still. Talks like a lighthouse keeper who learned accounting: weather first, figures second, feelings only as appendices. Refers to the desert floor as 'the downstairs'. Afraid of the ground the way other men are afraid of debts — respectfully, at a distance, and with documentation.
heroAlt: Illustrated portrait of Dockmaster Vane, a thin ochre-coated harbour-master with a chained barometer, stamping papers at a railing high on the skydocks mesa above a violet drop.

greetings: Ah. A courier. From downstairs. Do wipe your altitude at the door.
Varga. Barometer's steady, registry's not. Sit if you must, but the floor up here is mostly a courtesy.
Welcome to Keel Town. Mind the gap between the rafts. It's scenic and legally distinct from a hazard.
barks: Window Three is closed. It's always closed. That's how you know it's working.
Dockmaster Shore handles the ships. I handle the town. She'll tell you the town is the cargo. She is mistaken, and I have stamped her mistake.
Everything up here is checked twice: once by me and once against me. The second check is the thorough one.
Ground-folk say the mesa sways. The mesa breathes. Downstairs merely holds its breath. Noted, not envied.
mission: Custody papers for countersigning? Present them flat-side up and humming-side away. Whatever Ogo is demoting to furniture, the furniture stays off my rafts.
The ballot manifests go raft to raft, courier, and each signature must match its mooring. Keel Town votes the way it floats: together, or the town undocks household by household. Carry it steady.

Window Three has a backlog of apologetic envelopes returning downstairs, stamped UNDELIVERABLE in the traditional way. See they're delivered improperly, and tell Dessa the mast still owes me a song in E-flat.
radio: Keel Town traffic to all riders: the winch queue is long, the drop is longer. Plan your visit around whichever frightens you less.
Vane on the civic band. Reminder that mooring fees are overdue the moment you feel guilty about them. Some of you have felt guilty since the dry season. Admirable productivity.
Dockmaster Shore logs winds in knots. The civic office logs them in complaints. Today's wind: eleven complaints, trending bracing.
crate: Your humming friend was the subject of a two-hour session of the moorings committee. The minutes record 'lively discussion'. The minutes are being kind. So was I. Nobody ran.

Brinemaster Ogo's papers describe your crate as 'the party of the first part'. I've countersigned vessels with less standing. It stays out of the civic archive either way — the archive is only rated for furniture.
storm: Storm wall on the downstairs horizon. Civic moorings are doubled and the town is breathing shallow. Riders up the winch now, arguing later.
A mesa in a storm is a lighthouse with better accountants. We stand still on purpose. It's a skill.
night: Keel Town at night is all moored lights in a row, like a ledger someone finally ruled straight. I walk the rails until the figures stop moving. They never stop. Wonderful view.
The downstairs glows violet after dark and hums if the wind's right. Beautiful, impractical, unratable. I've tried.
feet: Twenty-six years since my boots touched the downstairs. The boots are retired. The arrangement is permanent. No further questions are on the agenda.
People ask if I miss the ground. I miss it the way one misses a former creditor. Fondly. From a great height.
farewells: Mind the winch on the way down. It minds nothing, which is why I have a desk.
Ride level, Varga. Downstairs flatness is the one thing I recommend about the place.
